primary_secondary.claude: no explicit basis (structured curation of scientific literature and public company sources into a metrics dataset, i.e. a mapping-type synthesis, plus a new web tool)
primary_secondary.nlm: Primary (mixed methods: curation plus 20+ interviews; 'empirical dataset')
primary_secondary.note: Claude describes a curation of existing literature and company sources (secondary-like) that also yields a new tool and dataset; NotebookLM frames it as primary mixed methods. Neither settles Primary vs Secondary.

study_type.claude: Other (tool and curated metrics dataset; magazine article)
study_type.nlm: Mixed methods (curation of literature and 50+ organizations' practices plus qualitative interviews with 20+ leaders)
study_type.note: Claude treats it as a tool/dataset paper with a fictional illustrative scenario; NotebookLM as mixed methods. The interviews with 20+ leaders are mentioned once, with no method described.

research_method.claude: Structured curation of scientific literature and public company resources (blogs, talks, case studies, podcasts) with multi-dimension annotation of each metric and descriptive statistics; open-source web tool illustrated by a fictional scenario ('Alex'); interviews with 20+ leaders mentioned without method
research_method.nlm: Mixed methods: structured content analysis/curation of scientific literature and public practices of 50+ organizations, plus qualitative interviews with 20+ DevEx and engineering leaders
research_method.value: Structured curation of scientific literature and public company resources (engineering blogs, conference talks, case studies, podcasts) from 50+ organizations into a dataset of 120+ DevEx metrics annotated by data-collection type, collection maturity, origin, AI relevance and outcome goal, summarized with descriptive statistics; released as the open-source DevEx Metrics Compass web tool; interviews with 20+ DevEx and engineering leaders mentioned without a described method
research_method.note: Fictional scenario omitted: NotebookLM reports the 'Alex' outcomes (higher cognitive load, PR size nearly doubled) as empirical findings, while Claude marks them as an illustrative example. No search strategy, inclusion criteria or annotation procedure is reported.

context.claude: Mixed; academic authors (UZH, UBC) analysing research and industry sources; 120+ metrics from literature and 50+ organizations; 20+ leaders interviewed
context.nlm: Mixed; industry engineering organizations (tech, fintech, enterprise) plus academic SE research; 120+ metrics, 50+ organizations, 20+ expert interviews
context.value: mixed; scientific literature plus public measurement practices of 50+ engineering organizations (e.g., Google, Microsoft, Atlassian, Spotify, Capital One, Stripe); 120+ metrics; interviews with 20+ DevEx and engineering leaders
context.note: NotebookLM's 'fintech' sector comes from the fictional Alex scenario. The number of papers reviewed is not reported.

dora_applied.claude: No (referenced; used as an origin label for metrics in the dataset)
dora_applied.nlm: Yes ('referenced & applied': provides the standard delivery-performance metrics)
dora_applied.note: Full text: the Compass is 'built on top of, and complementary to' DORA, SPACE and DX Core 4, and DORA metrics are among the most-referenced metrics in the dataset; no measurement is done with DORA.

space_applied.note: SPACE referenced as inspiration ('beyond single-framework thinking') only.

ai_discussed.note: Measuring AI impact is the article's motivation; AI-specific metrics (adoption rate, acceptance rate, % AI-generated code, AI spend) and an AI-relevance annotation in the dataset.

remote_covid.note: Work mode not reported by either; not mentioned in the full text.

cat_productivity.note: Throughput (27 sources) and produced code (25) reported as the main output-oriented metrics; perceived productivity also listed (survey).

cat_quality.note: Change failure rate (27), MTTR (16), code rework rate; quality is one of the eight dimensions.

cat_collaboration.claude: Yes (collaboration quality listed as a self-reported team/developer-enablement metric)
cat_collaboration.nlm: No (no collaboration metric; collaboration only named as a neglected human dimension)
cat_collaboration.note: Full text: 'Collaboration quality, autonomy, learning and development, and cognitive load all require data collection through surveys or interviews'; the team dimension (collaboration, communication) is flagged as understudied.

cat_satisfaction.note: Developer satisfaction is the most referenced metric (45 sources); well-being metrics (cognitive load, focus time, interruptions); NotebookLM also lists burnout risk score.

cat_activity.note: Commits, PR counts, LOC and produced code discussed as easy-to-collect, gameable activity metrics; produced code among the most referenced.

cat_delivery.note: Deployment frequency (21) and cycle time (19) among the most referenced metrics.

cat_devex.note: DevEx framework (Noda et al.) only referenced; cognitive load and focus time appear as dataset well-being metrics, not via the framework.

cat_agile.note: The Compass has a 'process' dimension, but neither extractor reports sprint/scrum/workflow metrics.

cat_survey.note: Self-reported (survey/interview) collection type is a dataset annotation; periodic surveys argued as essential alongside telemetry.

evidence.quote: To understand how DevEx is actually measured across both research and industry, we conducted a structured curation effort.

This consisted of reviewing scientific literature alongside public company resources: engineering blogs, conference talks, case studies, and podcasts from more than 50 organizations, including Google, Microsoft, Atlassian, Spotify, Capital One, and Stripe.
The result is a dataset of 120-plus metrics organized across eight dimensions: developer enablement, system, process, business, quality, team, output, and customer.
Interviews with more than 20 DevEx and engineering leaders consistently surfaced the same frustration

As AI-augmented development becomes standard practice, engineering leaders face mounting pressure to demonstrate its impact. Yet most organizations are measuring AI adoption and output while the effect on developer experience (DevEx) remains largely unknown.
Two widely applied outputoriented measures are throughput (27 times) and produced code (25 times).
The (original four) DORA metrics follow closely: change failure rate (27 times), deployment frequency (21 times), cycle time (19 times), and MTTR (16 times)
Developer satisfaction is the most broadly referenced metric overall, appearing in 45 sources.
Automated metrics, such as number of commits, PR counts, AI token spend, and lines of code (LoC), are abundant and cheap to collect.
For that, self-reported (qualitative) signals are essential: Periodic surveys and targeted follow-up interviews surface the human experience behind the numbers
